## Welcome {#home}

### Hypertension

**Learning Objectives:**

- Describe the global and Indian burden of hypertension
- Define hypertension and classify it by severity
- Identify risk factors for hypertension
- Apply primary and secondary prevention to hypertension control

🟢 **MUST KNOW** · 🟡 **SHOULD KNOW** · 🟣 **MAY KNOW** · 🧡 **QUESTION**

::: {.notes}
Hypertension is both a disease in its own right and the single largest
modifiable risk factor for stroke, covered next — the two modules are
best read together.
:::

---

## Definition and Burden {background-color="#E3F2E1"}

🟢 **MUST KNOW**

**Hypertension** is diagnosed when, on **two separate days**, systolic
BP ≥140 mmHg and/or diastolic BP ≥90 mmHg.

- **Global:** ~1.13 billion people affected, two-thirds in low- and
  middle-income countries; prevalence over 60% in people aged 60+
- **India (NFHS 2015–16):** 15% of men, 11% of women hypertensive;
  prevalence rises consistently with BMI
- Called the **"silent killer"** — most affected people have no symptoms
  and are unaware of their status, which is why regular BP measurement
  matters more than symptom-based detection

**Global NCD target:** reduce hypertension prevalence by 25% by 2025
(2010 baseline).

---

## Classification {background-color="#E3F2E1"}

🟢 **MUST KNOW**

| Category | Systolic (mmHg) | Diastolic (mmHg) |
|---|---|---|
| Optimal | <120 | <80 |
| Normal | 120–129 | <85 |
| High-normal | 130–139 | 85–89 |
| Grade 1 (mild) | 140–159 | 90–99 |
| Grade 2 (moderate–severe) | ≥160 | ≥100 |

**When symptoms do occur** (usually only at higher grades): early
morning headache, nosebleeds, irregular heart rhythm, vision changes,
tinnitus; severe hypertension can cause fatigue, nausea, confusion, and
chest pain.

---

## Risk Factors and Prevention {background-color="#FFF6DA"}

🟡 **SHOULD KNOW**

**Risk factors:** age, sex, genetic factors, ethnicity, obesity, high
salt intake, alcohol use, physical inactivity, environmental stress.

- **Primary prevention** — reduce population-wide incidence through low
  salt diet, regular exercise, stress reduction, and weight/BMI control
- **Secondary prevention** — early case detection (routine BP screening)
  plus antihypertensive drug therapy once diagnosed

**Treatment approach:** lifestyle modification and stress management as
the foundation, with antihypertensive medication (e.g. amlodipine,
telmisartan, chlorthalidone — representative drug classes, not a
prescribing guide) added for confirmed hypertension.

## Self-Check: Question 1 {background-color="#FDE8E8"}

🧡 **QUESTION**

::: {.quiz-question}
### Question 1

A diagnosis of hypertension requires elevated readings measured:

- Once, at any single visit
- [On two separate days]{.correct data-explanation="Hypertension is diagnosed only when systolic ≥140 and/or diastolic ≥90 mmHg is confirmed on two separate days — a single elevated reading is not diagnostic."}
- Only in the morning
- After a 12-hour fast
:::

---

## Self-Check: Question 2 {background-color="#FDE8E8"}

🧡 **QUESTION**

::: {.quiz-question}
### Question 2

Hypertension is often called the "silent killer" because:

- It always causes sudden death
- [Most affected people have no symptoms and are unaware of their condition]{.correct data-explanation="The majority of people with hypertension have no warning signs or symptoms, which is exactly why routine BP screening — not symptom-based detection — is the public health strategy."}
- It is untreatable
- Symptoms only appear after death
:::

---

## Self-Check: Question 3 {background-color="#FDE8E8"}

🧡 **QUESTION**

::: {.quiz-question}
### Question 3

Reducing population salt intake to lower hypertension incidence is an
example of:

- Secondary prevention
- Tertiary prevention
- [Primary prevention]{.correct data-explanation="Reducing salt intake population-wide targets the risk factor before disease develops, the definition of primary prevention — distinct from secondary prevention (early detection) or tertiary (managing established disease)."}
- Screening
:::
